slides.text: For four years, I checked out the same decaying copy of 'Pride and Prejudice' from the university library. Not to read Austen, but to read him. It started when I scribbled a frustrated note in the margin about Mr. Darcy’s arrogance. The next week, I found a reply in elegant blue ink: 'He’s just terrified. Aren't we all?' We became margin-ghosts, confessing our deepest fears in the cramped white spaces of chapter seven, never knowing each other's names.

The blue ink became my lifeline. When my mother died, he wrote an original poem on page eighty that made me sob until I couldn't breathe. When I failed my finals, he drew a tiny, cheering knight on the title page. I started spending every afternoon near the classic literature section, desperately scanning the hands of passing students, looking for blue ink stains. But graduation was looming. In chapter forty, I finally wrote, 'Meet me by the fountain at noon.'

I waited at the fountain for three hours. No one came. Crushed, I returned to the library to return the book one last time. As I slid it onto the cart, a hand caught my wrist. It was the quiet, infuriatingly handsome archivist I had argued with daily about overdue fines. His fingers were smudged with brilliant blue ink. He handed me a folded page. 'I was terrified,' he whispered. 'But you're my favorite story. Please don't close the book.'
